courses.subject: BUDS
courses.title: Tiantai Buddhism
courses.description: The course explores the history, doctrines, thoughts, and literature of Tiantai Buddhism in China. It includes a study of the historical development of the Tiantai tradition in medieval China with an analysis of major figures and their interactions with Chinese cultural tradition. Readings will include both primary and secondary sources.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MA Buddhist Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:

Upon completing this module successfully, students should be able to

(1) demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the historical development, doctrines and practices of Chan/Zen school of Buddhism in China

(2) engage in a critical analysis of Chan/Zen Buddhism by the methods of the humanities and social sciences

Skill Outcomes

Upon completing this module successfully, students should be able to

(1) develop their analytical and problem solving ability, critical intelligence and appreciative thinking as well as key research skills and to prepare for advanced studies in religion.

(2) develop their social and interpersonal skills and ability to work collaboratively in a team.

Attitude Outcomes

Upon completing this module successfully, students should be able to

(1) recognize the contested and provisional nature of knowledge and understanding.

(2) develop tolerance of diverse positions and have respect for other’s view

(3) develop sensitivity to ultimate concern and religious dimension of human life

courses.subject: BUDS
courses.title: Chinese Buddhist Art
courses.description: This course surveys the historical development of Buddhist visual and material culture in pre-modern China from a trans-Asiatic perspective. Major topics include (1) characteristics of Buddhist image-making practice in China, especially vis-à-vis that of the Indian subcontinent, (2) the growth of Buddhist sculpture as a dominant artistic genre, (3) the inroads of foreign iconography and styles and their impact on China, (4) the emergence of Buddhist ritual architecture, including Sinicized cave temples and pagodas, (5) the issues of regional and period styles, and (6) the socio-political contexts of artistic production. The course will incorporate recent archaeological discoveries from the last six decades.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MA in Buddhist Studies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
The course helps students:

1. obtain a broad knowledge of Buddhist Studies as a discipline and a more specialized knowledge in analyzing individual works of painting, sculpture, and architecture created in pre-modern China.

2. identify regional variances, trans-regional diffusions, inter-regional commonalities, and historical transformations among cultures of the pan-Buddhist world.

3. develop an understanding of Buddhism in its philosophical and historical context with special reference to pre-modern China.

4. develop research skills in Buddhist Studies, including their competence in academic writing and presentation in order to prepare them for further academic research in Buddhist Studies.

5. develop a reflective and empathetic attitude in understanding Buddhism.

courses.subject: BUDS
courses.title: Buddhism and Contemporary Society
courses.description: In its long history of more than 2500 years, Buddhism has spread to most parts of the world, and its doctrines and practices have also undergone tremendous changes. This course is designed to study Buddhism within the framework of its developments in contemporary society. It explores a variety of topics, discussing Buddhist attitudes to and connections with modern society with respect to ecology, psychology, feminism, etc. In each of these topics, we will examine how Buddhism has fitted itself and been reinvented to make it meaningful and useful in serving people today. It is hoped that through comparative and critical analysis, students will be able to get familiar with Buddhist ideas and thoughts concerning social issues in diverse contemporary contexts.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MA in Buddhist Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To understand Buddhist attitude to and connections with contemporary society in various historical settings and contemporary contexts.

2. To examine in what ways Buddhism transforms contemporary society and culture, and vice versa.

3. To engage in a critical analysis of how Buddhism has accommodated itself with the modernization movements, and been reinvented to make it meaningful and useful to people nowadays.

4. To relate students’ personal growth and everyday life to Buddhist teachings so as to cultivate a constructive outlook on self-understanding and interpersonal relationship.

courses.subject: BUDS
courses.title: Basic Pāli
courses.description: This is an introductory course designed for those with no previous knowledge of the language of Pāli. The purpose of this course is to equip students with a basic understanding of Pāli so that they could read the Pāli primary source with a dictionary. It also enables them to understand Buddhist Sūtras compiled in Pāli. Course contents include: Pāli phonetics, parts of speech, different nouns and their declension, different verbs and their conjugation, participles and their function, absolutives, sandhi, syntax and classification of sentences.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MA in Buddhist Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:
(a) demonstrate a clear understanding of basic Pāli grammar, including phonetics, parts of speech, nouns of different gender and their declensions, verbs and their conjugations, participles and their functions, syntax and classification of sentences.
(b) apply the knowledge and skills acquired to read simple Pāli sentences and understand their religious and philosophical significance in context.
(c) Gain access to the Pāli primary source with a Pali dictionary.
courses.course_syllabus:
Text book: A. P. Buddhadatta, 1997. The New Pali Course, Part I. Colombo: Buddhist Cultural Centre.
Medium of Instruction: 中文普通话/English

Lesson 1: Introduction:
(a) A brief introduction to Pāli language and Pāli literature.
(b) Pāli Alphabets.
(c) Reading “Ti-saraṇa” (Three Refuges) in Pāli.

Lesson 2:
(a) Introduction to the Parts of Speech, Gender Number and Case in Pāli.
(b) Declension of Nouns: “a” ending Masculine Nouns.
(c) Exercise 1.
(d) Reading ‘pañcasīla’ (Five Precepts) in Pāli.

Lesson 3：
(a) Different Classes of Verbs and Conjugational Signs.
(b) The 1st Conjugation (Bhuvādigaṇa: “a”): Present Tense.
(c) The 7th Conjugation (Curādigaṇa: “e” and “aya”): Present Tense.
(d) Exercises 2-3.
(e) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 4:
(a) The 5th Conjugation (Kiyādigaṇa: “ṇā”).
(b) Conjugation of Verbs: Past Tense.
(c) Declension of Nouns – “I” ending Masculine Nouns.
(d) Exercise 4-5.
(e) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 5:
(a) Personal Pronouns.
(b) Irregular roots of 1st and 7th conjugations.
(c) Rule of Vowel Gradation.
(d) Exercise 6.
(e) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 6:
(a) Conjugation of Verbs: Future Tense.
(b) Declension of Nouns: “ī” and “u” ending Masculine Nouns.
(c) Adverbs of time and place.
(d) Exercises 7-8.
(e) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 7:
(a) Declension of irregular masculine nouns and adjectives ending in “u” – “bhatu” (brother) “nattu” (grandson), and “-vantu”, “- mantu”.
(b) The prepositions “saha (with)” and “saddhiṃ (with)”, and the conjunction “ca” (and), “api” or “pi”, “vā (or)”, etc.
(c) Exercises 9.
(d) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 8:
(a) Declension of Masculine Nouns with “ū” Ending.
(b) More Adverbs of Time.
(c) Exercise 10.
(d) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 9:
(a) Declension of Feminine Nouns with “ā” Ending.
(b) Conjugation of Verbs: Imperative and Optative.
(c) Exercise 11.
(d) Reading simple Pāli passages for the understanding of basic Buddhist concepts.

Lesson 10:
(a) Declension of Feminine Nouns with “I” and “ī” Endings.
(b) Conjugation of verbs: Indeclinable Past Participle (Absolutive).
(c) Exercise 12.
(d) Reading “Dhammacakkapavattana-sutta” (The Buddha’s First Sermon).

Lesson 11:
(a) Declension of Feminine Nouns with “u” Ending.
(b) Declension of irregular feminine nouns with "u" ending, such as ‘mātu’ (mother) “dhītu” (daughter) and so on.
(c) More Adverbs of Place.
(d) Exercise 13.
(e) Continue the Reading of ‘Dhammacakkapavattana-sutta’.
Lesson 12:
(a) Declension of Neuter Nouns with “a”, "i" and "u" Endings .
(b) Conjugation of verbs: Infinitive.
(c) More Pronounces.
(d) Exercise 14 and 15
(e) Reading simple Pāli passages.

3. knowledge and understanding of the basic Sanskrit structures and expressions.

4. the ability to understand simple narrative texts in written Sanskrit on topics of Buddhism.

5. the capability and awareness of utilizing a classical language in Buddhist studies.

courses.subject: BUDS
courses.title: Buddhism and Religious Culture in China
courses.description: This course offers an advanced introduction to the impact brought about by Buddhism to the religious culture in China. We will examine in-depth four key moments of paradigm shift in Chinese religious culture, in the Warring States Period (481-256 BC) before the arrival of Buddhism, the Period of Division (220-589 AD), the Song-Yuan (960-1368), and modern China (1850-present). One focus of the course is to investigate how Buddhism interacted with local religious culture in China through a variety of confluences and conflicts in relationship to changing social, political, and economic systems. We will review foundational debates from the 20th century, such as ‘Buddhist conquest of China’ and ‘Chinese transformation of Buddhism’ or the ‘Sinification of Buddhism.’
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MA in Buddhist Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
On successful completion of the module students will be able to:

1. demonstrate an advanced critical knowledge of the historical development of Buddhism in China from its introduction around the turn of the Common Era through the new challenges it has faced in modern China (1850-present).
2. situate Buddhism as a part of Chinese religious tradition in its relationship with indigenous beliefs and practices;
3. know how Buddhist universalism transformed the native Daoist religion and society, contributing to fundamental changes in the vision of self and the practice of government, as well as alternative lifestyles and forms of social empowerment for women.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. The Issue of definition and unified whole
2. Kinship-based ancestor worship and Shamanism of the Royal period
3. The Emergence of Self-Cultivation Practice and Qi-based Cosmology in Warring States
4. State Religion in Period of Political Unity
5. Paradigm shift and Religious transformations brought in by Buddhism
6. Scripture and the Three Religions
7. Literature and the Three Religions
8. The Three Religions in the Song
9. Temple-centric society since the Song: Rural versus Urban
10. Buddhism for the Elite versus Popular
11. Modern attack on religion and the Buddhist reform in the Twentieth Century
12. Gender and the Buddhist alternative lifestyles and empowerment for women
13. Buddhist Conquest of China or Sinification of Buddhism
